languages-english.title: Bhasha: Spoken English
languages-english.description: Spoken English from first words to fluent, confident conversation — everyday situations, clear pronunciation, job interviews and an honest IELTS overview, built for Indian learners.

courses.title: Spoken English 1: Start speaking
courses.summary: Greet people, introduce yourself, talk about your daily routine, ask questions and tell a simple story about the past — with the most common mistakes Indian learners make and how to fix them.
outcomes: Learners can greet and introduce themselves naturally
Learners can describe routines using the present simple correctly (he/she/it + s)
Learners can form yes/no and wh- questions
Learners can tell a short story using the past simple, including common irregular verbs

story.title: Ravi's first day at the call centre

scenes.text: Ravi, 21, from a Hindi-medium school in Gorakhpur, joins a customer-support training batch in Noida.
On day one the trainer says, 'Introduce yourselves.' Ravi says, 'Myself Ravi. I am belonging to Gorakhpur.' A few people smile.
Trainer Anita gently shows a simpler way: 'Hi, I'm Ravi. I'm from Gorakhpur.'
By Friday Ravi greets everyone confidently. 'Simple is correct,' he writes in his notebook.

steps.title: Greetings for every situation
steps.body:
- **Formal**: 'Good morning' (until about 12 noon), 'Good afternoon' (12 noon to about 5 pm), 'Good evening' (after about 5 pm). 'Good night' is only for saying goodbye at night or before sleep — not as a greeting.
- **Neutral/informal**: 'Hello', 'Hi', 'Hey' (very casual).
- **How are you?** → 'I'm fine, thanks. And you?' / 'Pretty good, thanks!' / 'Not bad.'
- **Meeting for the first time**: 'Nice to meet you.' → 'Nice to meet you too.'
- **Leaving**: 'Bye', 'See you tomorrow', 'Take care', 'Have a nice day'.

steps.title: A natural self-introduction
steps.body:
'Hi, I'm **Priya**. I'm from **Madurai**, and I live in **Chennai** now. I'm a **second-year BCom student**. In my free time I **like reading and playing badminton**. Nice to meet you!'

Pattern: name → place → work/study → one or two interests → friendly close.

steps.title: Common mistakes and fixes
steps.body:
- 'Myself Ravi.' → **'I'm Ravi.'** or 'My name is Ravi.'
- 'I am belonging to Gorakhpur.' → **'I'm from Gorakhpur.'**
- 'What is your good name?' → **'What's your name?'** or 'May I know your name?'
- 'I am having two brothers.' → **'I have two brothers.'** (have/know/like/belong are usually not used in -ing form for states)
- 'Good night' as a hello at 8 pm → **'Good evening.'**

steps.title: How to practise
steps.body: Record your introduction on your phone. Listen. Is it clear? Is it under 30 seconds? Say it five times a day for a week until it feels natural — then change one detail each day so you're not memorising, you're speaking.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your own introduction using the pattern: name, place, work/study, two interests, friendly close. Say it aloud to a mirror or a friend.

activity.prompt: Match the situation with the best phrase.
pairs: Meeting your new manager at 10 am
Good morning, nice to meet you.
Leaving a friend's house at night

quiz.q: Which is the most natural introduction?
quiz.why: The answer is "I'm Kiran.". Reason: 'I'm Kiran' or 'My name is Kiran' is natural English. The other choices, such as "Me Kiran is." and "Kiran myself only.", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: At 7 pm you meet a colleague. You say…
quiz.why: The answer is "Good evening". Reason: 'Good night' is for leaving or bedtime. The other choices, such as "Good morning" and "Good afternoon", do not fit the question.
The answer is "I have a sister.". Reason: 'Have' for possession is usually not used in -ing form. The other choices, such as "I am have a sister." and "I having sister.", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Best reply to 'Nice to meet you'?
quiz.why: The answer is "Nice to meet you too". Reason: 'Nice to meet you too' is standard. The other choices, such as "Okay" and "Thanks for meeting", do not fit the question.
The answer is "Where you come from". Reason: 'From' indicates origin. The other choices, such as "Your age" and "Your job", do not fit the question. (Question: 'I'm from Kochi' tells people…)

scenes.text: Meera, a nurse in Bhubaneswar, joins an online English club. The task: describe your daily routine.
She says, 'My husband go to office at nine. He take bus.' The tutor nods and writes something.
'Add -s for he, she and it,' the tutor explains: 'He goes. He takes the bus.'
Next week Meera describes her whole family's routine without a single -s mistake.

steps.title: When to use the present simple
steps.body:
Use it for **habits, routines, facts and timetables**:

- 'I **wake up** at 6.' (habit)
- 'She **works** in a hospital.' (fact about life)
- 'Water **boils** at 100 °C.' (general truth)
- 'The train **leaves** at 8:15.' (timetable)

Time words: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never, every day, on Mondays.

steps.title: The he/she/it rule
steps.body:
With **he, she, it** (or one person/thing), add **-s** or **-es**:

- work → works, play → plays
- go → **goes**, do → **does**, watch → watches, fix → fixes
- study → **studies** (consonant + y → -ies)
- have → **has**

I/you/we/they: no -s ('They work', 'We go').

steps.title: Negatives and questions
steps.body:
- Negative: **don't / doesn't + base verb**. 'I don't eat meat.' 'He **doesn't** eat meat.' (not 'doesn't eats')
- Question: **Do / Does + subject + base verb**? 'Do you like tea?' '**Does** she live here?' (not 'Does she lives')

Once you use **does/doesn't**, the main verb loses its -s.

steps.title: Where frequency words go
steps.body:
Usually **before the main verb**: 'I **usually** take the bus.' 'She **never** drinks coffee.'

But **after 'be'**: 'He is **always** late.' 'We are **often** tired on Mondays.'

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Describe a family member's day in six sentences using he or she. Underline every verb and check the -s.

activity.prompt: Complete with the correct present simple form.
activity.text: My father ___ (go) to work at 9. He ___ (not/drive); he ___ (take) the metro. ___ (do) your sister work?

options: She is work in a bank.
quiz.why: The answer is "She works in a bank.". Reason: He/she/it takes -s. The other choices, such as "She is work in a bank." and "She working in bank.", do not fit the question.
The answer is "He doesn't like tea.". Reason: Doesn't + base verb. The other choices, such as "He doesn't likes tea." and "He don't like tea.", do not fit the question.
The answer is "studies". Reason: Consonant + y → -ies. The other choices, such as "study" and "studys", do not fit the question. (Question: 'Study' with 'she' becomes…)
The answer is "is always". Reason: Frequency words go after 'be'. The other choices, such as "is late always is" and "always", do not fit the question.
The answer is "Does he live here?". Reason: Does + subject + base verb. The other choices, such as "He lives here does?" and "Does he lives here?", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Abdul, newly arrived in Bengaluru for a job, needs to find a bank, a SIM card shop and a bus to Whitefield.
He knows English words but freezes when forming questions: 'Where bank is?'
His flatmate teaches him one pattern: question word + do/does/is/are + subject + verb.
By evening he's asked ten questions correctly — and found everything.

steps.title: Yes/no questions
steps.body:
- With **be**: move **is/are/am** before the subject. 'You are ready.' → '**Are you** ready?'
- With other verbs: add **do/does**. 'You like cricket.' → '**Do you** like cricket?'
- With **can/will/should**: move it first. 'She can swim.' → '**Can she** swim?'

Short answers: 'Yes, I am.' 'No, I don't.' 'Yes, she can.'

steps.title: Wh- questions
steps.body:
Pattern: **Wh- word + auxiliary + subject + verb?**

- What do you do? (= What's your job?)
- Where **is** the bank?
- When **does** the bus leave?
- Why **are** you late?
- How **much** is this? How **many** people are coming?
- Which bus goes to Whitefield? Who called you?

steps.title: Common mistakes and fixes
steps.body:
- 'Where bank is?' → **'Where is the bank?'**
- 'What you want?' → **'What do you want?'** (or more polite: 'What would you like?')
- 'Why you are late?' → **'Why are you late?'**
- 'You are coming, na?' (Indian tag) → in formal English: **'You're coming, aren't you?'** or simply 'Are you coming?'
- 'Can you tell me where is the station?' → **'Can you tell me where the station is?'** (in indirect questions, no inversion)

steps.title: Polite question starters
steps.body:
- 'Excuse me, could you tell me…?'
- 'Do you know where … is?'
- 'Would you mind…?'
- 'Is it possible to…?'

Polite forms matter in offices, banks and with strangers.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write 8 questions you'd ask a new classmate or colleague: 2 yes/no with be, 2 with do/does, 4 wh- questions. Ask a friend and listen to their answers.

activity.prompt: Put the words in the correct order to make a question: 'When / the / does / leave / bus?'

quiz.why: The answer is "Where is the bank?". Reason: Wh- + be + subject. The other choices, such as "Where bank is?" and "Bank where is?", do not fit the question.
The answer is "Does she like mangoes?". Reason: Does + subject + base verb. The other choices, such as "She likes mangoes does?" and "Does she likes mangoes?", do not fit the question.

options: Can you tell me where is the station?
Can you tell me where the station is?
quiz.why: The answer is "Can you tell me where the station is?". Reason: No inversion in indirect questions. The other choices, such as "Can you tell where station?" and "Can you tell me where is the station?", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Most polite way to ask a stranger?
options: Excuse me, could you tell me where the restroom is?
quiz.why: The answer is "Excuse me, could you tell me where the restroom is?". Reason: Polite starters matter. The other choices, such as "Tell me toilet." and "Where is toilet?", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: To ask about quantity of uncountable things use…
quiz.why: The answer is "How much". Reason: How much money/water/time. The other choices, such as "How many" and "How long", do not fit the question. (Question: To ask about quantity of uncountable things use…)

lessons.title: Telling what happened: the past simple

scenes.text: Sneha from Nagpur tells her friend about her campus interview: 'I go there, I give test, they ask many questions.'
Her friend asks, 'Is it happening now, or did it happen yesterday?'
Sneha learns the past simple: 'I went there, I took a test, and they asked lots of questions.'
Her storytelling becomes clear — and she gets the job in the next round.

steps.title: Regular verbs: add -ed
steps.body:
Use the past simple for **finished actions at a finished time**: yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago.

- work → worked, play → played, ask → asked
- live → lived (just add -d)
- study → studied (consonant + y → -ied)
- stop → stopped (short verbs: double the last consonant)

Pronunciation of -ed: /t/ in 'asked, worked'; /d/ in 'played, called'; /ɪd/ in 'wanted, needed' (after t or d).

steps.title: Common irregular verbs (learn these first)
steps.body: go → **went**, come → **came**, see → **saw**, take → **took**, give → **gave**, get → **got**, make → **made**, have → **had**, do → **did**, say → **said**, tell → **told**, eat → **ate**, buy → **bought**, think → **thought**, write → **wrote**, speak → **spoke**, meet → **met**, find → **found**, leave → **left**, be → **was/were**.

steps.title: Negatives and questions in the past
steps.body:
Use **did / didn't + base verb**:

- 'I **didn't go**.' (not 'didn't went')
- '**Did** you **see** the match?' (not 'Did you saw')
- 'Where **did** you **buy** it?'

With **be**: 'I **wasn't** there.' '**Were** you at home?'

steps.title: Linking words for stories
steps.body:
**First**, … **Then**, … **After that**, … **Suddenly**, … **Finally**, …

'**First**, I reached the office at nine. **Then** I took a written test. **After that**, they called me for an interview. **Finally**, they said I was selected!'

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Tell the story of your last weekend in 6–8 sentences using linking words. Record it and count the past-tense verbs.

The answer is "I didn't go.". Reason: Didn't + base verb. The other choices, such as "I didn't went." and "I not went.", do not fit the question. (Question: Correct negative:)
The answer is "Did you see it?". Reason: Did + subject + base verb. The other choices, such as "Did you saw it?" and "Saw you it?", do not fit the question.
The answer is "/ɪd/ (an extra syllable)". Reason: After t or d, -ed adds a syllable. The other choices, such as "Silent" and "/d/", do not fit the question.
The answer is "bought". Reason: Buy → bought (bring → brought). The other choices, such as "buy" and "brought", do not fit the question. (Question: Past of 'buy'?)

questions.why: The answer is "I'm Arjun.". Reason: I'm / My name is. The other choices, such as "Arjun myself." and "Me Arjun.", do not fit the question. (Question: Most natural introduction:)
The answer is "Good morning". Reason: Morning greeting. The other choices, such as "Good afternoon" and "Good night", do not fit the question. (Question: At 8 am you say…)
The answer is "plays". Reason: He + -s. The other choices, such as "play" and "playing", do not fit the question. (Question: He ___ cricket every Sunday.)
The answer is "Where do you live?". Reason: Wh- + do + subject + verb. The other choices, such as "Where you are live?" and "Where does you live?", do not fit the question.
The answer is "took". Reason: Irregular. The other choices, such as "taked" and "tooked", do not fit the question. (Question: Past of 'take':)
The answer is "doesn't drink". Reason: Doesn't + base verb. The other choices, such as "don't drink" and "not drink", do not fit the question. (Question: 'She ___ coffee.' (negative))
The answer is "I know him.". Reason: 'Know' is a state verb. The other choices, such as "I am know him." and "I knowing him.", do not fit the question.

options: Where the office is do you know?
Do you know where is the office?
Do you know where the office is?
questions.why: The answer is "Do you know where the office is?". Reason: No inversion inside. The other choices, such as "Where the office is do you know?" and "Do you know where office?", do not fit the question.
The answer is "were". Reason: They + were. The other choices, such as "was" and "are", do not fit the question. (Question: 'They ___ at home yesterday.')

questions.q: Where does 'usually' go? 'I ___ take the bus.'
questions.why: The answer is "usually take". Reason: Before the main verb. The other choices, such as "take usually" and "am usually take", do not fit the question. (Question: Where does 'usually' go? 'I ___ take the bus.')
The answer is "Did she go home early?". Reason: Did + base verb. The other choices, such as "She didn't went home." and "Did she went home early?", do not fit the question.

options: My brother study in Pune and he doesn't likes hostel food.
My brother studys in Pune and he don't like hostel food.
My brother is study in Pune and he not like hostel food.
My brother studies in Pune and he doesn't like hostel food.
questions.why: The answer is "My brother studies in Pune and he doesn't like hostel food.". Reason: Studies; doesn't like. The other choices, such as "My brother study in Pune and he doesn't likes hostel food." and "My brother studys in Pune and he don't like hostel food.", do not fit the question.

courses.title: Spoken English 2: Everyday conversations
courses.summary: Handle real situations in English: shopping and bargaining, phone calls and messages, asking for directions and help while travelling, small talk and disagreeing politely.
outcomes: Learners can shop, ask prices, request changes and return items politely
Learners can make and receive phone calls and leave clear messages
Learners can ask for and give directions and handle travel problems
Learners can make small talk and disagree respectfully

scenes.text: Kavya bought running shoes at a mall in Hyderabad. At home, they were a size too small.
She worried about sounding rude when returning them.
Her cousin taught her a few polite phrases: 'I'd like to exchange these, please. They're too small.'
The staff exchanged them in two minutes. Kavya realised polite and clear is all you need.

steps.title: Useful shopping phrases
steps.body:
- 'How much is this?' / 'How much are these?'
- 'Do you have this in a bigger/smaller size?' / 'in blue?'
- 'Can I try it on?' → 'Where's the trial room / fitting room?'
- 'I'm just looking, thanks.'
- 'I'll take it.' / 'Can I pay by UPI / card?'
- 'Could I have a bill, please?'

steps.title: Returns, exchanges and complaints
steps.body:
- 'I'd like to **return** this, please. It doesn't fit.'
- 'Could I **exchange** it for a larger size?'
- 'There's a problem with this — it's **damaged / not working**.'
- 'I have the bill here.'
- 'Could I speak to the manager, please?' (calmly, if needed)

Polite structure: **problem → request → evidence → thanks**.

steps.title: Sample conversation
steps.body:
**Customer**: Excuse me, do you have this shirt in medium?
**Staff**: Let me check… Yes, here you are.
**Customer**: Thanks. Can I try it on?
**Staff**: Sure, the trial room is on the left.
**Customer**: It fits well. How much is it?
**Staff**: It's ₹1,299.
**Customer**: Is there any discount?
**Staff**: There's 10% off with this card.
**Customer**: Great, I'll take it. Can I pay by UPI?

steps.title: Numbers and prices
steps.body:
- ₹1,299 = 'one thousand two hundred (and) ninety-nine rupees' or 'twelve ninety-nine'.
- ₹2,50,000 = 'two lakh fifty thousand' (Indian system) = '250 thousand' (international).
- ₹1,00,00,000 = 'one crore' = '10 million'.
- Watch 'fifteen' (stress on -TEEN) vs 'fifty' (stress on FIF-) — a common confusion.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Role-play with a friend: one is the shopkeeper, one the customer. Do a purchase, then a return. Switch roles.

a.text: You bought earphones yesterday; the left side doesn't work. At the shop counter, you say…

choices.label: 'These are useless. Give my money back now!'
choices.feedback: Too aggressive — it makes the staff defensive.

choices.label: 'Hi, I bought these yesterday, but the left earphone isn't working. Could I exchange them?'

b1.text: The staff member becomes defensive: 'You must have broken them.' What now?

choices.label: Calm down: 'Sorry, I'm upset. Here's my bill — could you check them, please?'

b2.text: 'Do you have the bill?' asks the staff member.

choices.label: 'Why do you need a bill?'
choices.feedback: Shops usually need proof of purchase.

e1.text: The manager asks you to come back later. Calm, clear requests work better — try again.

e2.text: 'Thank you. Here's a new pair.' Polite + clear + proof = success.

e3.text: Without proof of purchase, they can't help. Keep bills for returns and warranty.

quiz.q: Polite way to ask for another size:
options: Do you have this in a larger size?
quiz.why: The answer is "Do you have this in a larger size?". Reason: Question form is polite. The other choices, such as "Give big size." and "Size bigger now.", do not fit the question.

options: I'm browsing, no help needed now
quiz.why: The answer is "I'm browsing, no help needed now". Reason: Browsing phrase. The other choices, such as "I want to buy" and "I'm blind", do not fit the question.
The answer is "250 thousand". Reason: 2.5 lakh = 250,000. The other choices, such as "2.5 million" and "25 thousand", do not fit the question. (Question: ₹2,50,000 in the international system is…)
The answer is "Problem → request → evidence → thanks". Reason: Clear and polite. The other choices, such as "Thanks → leave" and "Shout → demand → leave", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Rohit, a fresher in Pune, had to call a vendor to reschedule a delivery. He kept postponing it.
His senior, Fatima, gave him a script: greeting, who you are, why you're calling, request, confirm, thanks.
He practised twice, then called. It took 90 seconds.
'Scripts are training wheels,' said Fatima. 'Soon you won't need them.'

steps.title: Making a call: the structure
steps.body:
1. **Greet + identify**: 'Good morning, this is Rohit from ABC Pvt Ltd.'
2. **Check**: 'Am I speaking with Mr. Rao?' / 'Is this a good time to talk?'
3. **Reason**: 'I'm calling about the delivery scheduled for Friday.'
4. **Request**: 'Would it be possible to move it to Monday?'
5. **Confirm**: 'So that's Monday, 11 am, at our Baner office. Is that right?'
6. **Close**: 'Thank you so much. Have a good day.'

In English, say **'This is Rohit'** on the phone, not 'I am Rohit speaking'.

steps.title: Receiving calls and taking messages
steps.body:
- 'Hello, Sunrise Clinic, Priya speaking. How may I help you?'
- 'May I know who's calling?'
- 'Could you hold for a moment, please?'
- 'I'm afraid she's in a meeting. Can I take a message?'
- 'Could you spell that, please?' / 'Could you repeat the number?'
- Read back: 'Let me read that back to you…'

steps.title: Spelling clearly
steps.body: Use words for letters to avoid mistakes: **'B for Bombay, D for Delhi'**, or the international alphabet: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot… Say numbers in small groups: '98 45 – 678 – 123'.

steps.title: Professional messages (WhatsApp, email)
steps.body:
- Start with a greeting and your name if they may not know you.
- One message, complete thought — don't send 'Hi' and wait.
- Be clear about the ask and deadline.

Example: 'Hi Mr. Rao, this is Rohit from ABC. Could we move Friday's delivery to Monday 11 am? Please confirm when convenient. Thanks!'

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write and practise a 6-step script to call a clinic and book an appointment. Then practise taking a message for someone else.

activity.prompt: Put the professional phone call in order.
items: Good morning, this is Rohit from ABC Pvt Ltd.
Is this a good time to talk?
Would it be possible to move it to Monday?
So that's Monday, 11 am. Is that right?
Thank you so much. Have a good day.

quiz.q: On the phone, the natural way to say who you are:
quiz.why: The answer is "This is Rohit.". Reason: 'This is…' is standard on the phone. The other choices, such as "Myself Rohit calling." and "I am Rohit speaking here.", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: To check if someone can talk:
options: Is this a good time to talk?
quiz.why: The answer is "Is this a good time to talk?". Reason: Polite and professional. The other choices, such as "You free?" and "Listen.", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The person isn't available. You say…
options: I'm afraid she's not available. Can I take a message?
quiz.why: The answer is "I'm afraid she's not available. Can I take a message?". Reason: Polite and helpful. The other choices, such as "She is no." and "Call later.", do not fit the question.
The answer is "To confirm accuracy". Reason: Prevents errors. The other choices, such as "To waste time" and "It's rude", do not fit the question. (Question: Why read back details?)

lessons.title: Directions, travel and asking for help

scenes.text: Mr. and Mrs. Nair, retired teachers from Kollam, flew to visit their son in Canada with a stop in Dubai.
Their first flight was late, and they missed the connection.
Mrs. Nair walked to the transfer desk: 'Excuse me, we've missed our connecting flight to Toronto. Could you help us, please?'
They were rebooked within an hour. 'Clear English and a calm voice,' she said later, 'opened every door.'

steps.title: Asking for directions
steps.body:
- 'Excuse me, how do I get to the railway station?'
- 'Is there a pharmacy near here?'
- 'Which bus goes to MG Road?'
- 'How far is it?' / 'Is it walking distance?'
- 'Could you show me on the map?'

steps.title: Understanding directions
steps.body:
- 'Go **straight** for two blocks.'
- 'Turn **left/right** at the signal / at the second junction.'
- 'It's **opposite** the bank / **next to** the post office / **between** the school and the temple / **on your left**.'
- 'Take the second exit at the roundabout.'
- 'It's about five minutes' walk.'

steps.title: Travel problems
steps.body:
- 'My flight has been **cancelled/delayed**. What are my options?'
- 'I've **missed** my connection.'
- 'My bag **hasn't arrived**. Where do I report it?'
- 'I've **lost** my passport / wallet. Where is the nearest police station?'
- 'I need a doctor. Is there a hospital nearby?'
- At a hotel: 'I have a reservation under the name Nair.' / 'The AC in my room isn't working.'

steps.title: When you don't understand
steps.body:
It's completely normal. Say:

- 'Sorry, could you say that again, please?'
- 'Could you speak a little more slowly?'
- 'Do you mean…?'
- 'Could you write it down, please?'

Asking is smarter than guessing.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Using a map app, give a friend directions from your home to a nearby shop using at least five direction phrases. Then ask them to give directions back.

activity.prompt: Match the problem with the best sentence.
pairs: My flight has been cancelled. What are my options?
Sorry, could you say that again, please?

The AC in my room isn't working.
I need a doctor. Is there a hospital nearby?

options: Facing the bank, across the road
quiz.why: The answer is "Facing the bank, across the road". Reason: Opposite = facing, on the other side. The other choices, such as "Next to the bank" and "Inside the bank", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: You didn't catch what someone said. You say…
options: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
quiz.why: The answer is "Sorry, could you say that again, please?". Reason: Polite clarification. The other choices, such as "Huh?" and "Repeat!", do not fit the question.

options: I have a reservation under the name Nair.
quiz.why: The answer is "I have a reservation under the name Nair.". Reason: Standard phrase. The other choices, such as "Room me." and "I am Nair, room.", do not fit the question.

options: Whether you can walk there easily
quiz.why: The answer is "Whether you can walk there easily". Reason: Near enough to walk. The other choices, such as "The weather" and "The price", do not fit the question.

scenes.text: At a tech meetup in Gurugram, Nisha stood alone with her tea, not knowing how to start a conversation.
She tried a simple opener: 'Hi, I'm Nisha. Is this your first time at this meetup?'
The conversation flowed. Later, someone strongly said remote work is useless; Nisha disagreed politely: 'I see your point, but in my team it's worked well.'
She left with three new contacts and an invitation to speak next month.

steps.title: Starting small talk
steps.body:
Safe openers:

- 'Is this your first time here?'
- 'How do you know the host?'
- 'What brings you here today?'
- 'This weather is something, isn't it?'
- 'Have you tried the food? The samosas are great.'

Avoid early: salary, religion, politics, weight, marriage plans, caste.

steps.title: Keeping it going
steps.body:
- **Ask follow-up questions**: 'Oh, what kind of projects do you work on?'
- **Share a little**: 'I'm in data analytics myself.'
- **Show interest**: 'Really? That sounds interesting.' / 'How did you get into that?'
- **Close politely**: 'It was great talking to you. I'll go grab some food — see you around!'

steps.body:

- 'From my experience, …'
- '**Could it be that**…?'

Avoid: 'You're wrong.' 'That's stupid.' Attack the idea gently, never the person.

courses.title: Spoken English 3: Pronunciation and fluency
courses.summary: Speak clearly and confidently: tricky sounds for Indian speakers (v/w, th, z, schwa), word stress, sentence stress and intonation, linking, and daily habits that build real fluency. The goal is clarity, not a 'foreign' accent.
outcomes: Learners can produce v/w, th, z and the schwa sound clearly
Learners can place stress correctly in common words and noun/verb pairs

lessons.title: Tricky sounds: v/w, th, z and schwa

scenes.text: Varun, a software engineer in Hyderabad, presented to a client in London. He said 'wery well' for 'very well' and 'wision' for 'vision'.
The client was polite but asked him to repeat several words.
Varun practised with a mirror: upper teeth on lower lip for 'v', rounded lips for 'w'.
In the next call, the client said, 'Your explanation was very clear.' Varun smiled at the word 'very'.

steps.title: Clarity, not a new accent
steps.body: Indian English is a recognised, respected variety of English. You don't need to sound British or American. The goal is to be **clearly understood worldwide**. A few sounds cause most confusion — fix those, and keep your natural voice.

steps.title: /v/ vs /w/
steps.body:
- **/v/** (very, vision, village, seven): **upper teeth lightly touch the lower lip**, and you use your voice — it buzzes.
- **/w/** (well, water, wine, window): **round your lips** like saying 'oo', no teeth touching, then open.

Minimal pairs to practise: **vine – wine, vest – west, verse – worse, veil – whale**. Use a mirror.

steps.title: 'th': /θ/ and /ð/
steps.body:
- **/θ/** (think, three, thank, bath): tip of the tongue lightly **between the teeth**, blow air — no voice.
- **/ð/** (this, that, mother, the): same tongue position, **with voice**.

Many Indian speakers use a dental 't' or 'd' — usually understandable, but 'three' can sound like 'tree' and 'thin' like 'tin'. Practise: **three – tree, thin – tin, then – den**.

steps.title: /z/ and the schwa /ə/
steps.body:
- **/z/** buzzes like a bee: **zero, zoo, easy, busy, was, is, roses**. Avoid 'jero' or 'eaji'. Many plural -s endings are actually /z/: 'dogs', 'bags', 'plays'.
- **Schwa /ə/** is the most common sound in English — a short, relaxed 'uh' in **unstressed** syllables: **a**-bout, ban-**a**-n**a** (bə-NA-nə), doct-**or**, comm-**o**n, **to** (in 'go to work' = gə tə).

Pronouncing every vowel fully (ba-NA-NA) makes speech sound stiff.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Record yourself saying: 'Very well, thank you. I visited three villages with my mother on Thursday. It was easy and the weather was wonderful.' Listen for v/w, th and z. Re-record after a week of practice.

scenes.text: Ananya presented her project at a national seminar in Delhi. Some listeners looked confused at key words.
Her mentor played back the recording: 'You said deve-LOP-ment and e-co-NO-my.'
She learned to check stress in the dictionary — the mark ˈ comes before the stressed syllable.
At her next talk, people followed every point.

steps.title: What word stress is
steps.body:
In English, one syllable in a word is **stronger**: louder, longer and higher. The other syllables are weaker (often with schwa).

**PHO**-to-graph · pho-**TO**-gra-phy · pho-to-**GRA**-phic

Wrong stress can make a correct word hard to recognise — even more than a 'wrong' sound.

steps.title: Helpful patterns
steps.body:
- Many **two-syllable nouns and adjectives**: stress on the **first** syllable — **TA**-ble, **HAP**-py, **WA**-ter.
- Many **two-syllable verbs**: stress on the **second** — be-**GIN**, de-**CIDE**, re-**LAX**.
- **Noun/verb pairs**: a **RE**-cord (noun) / to re-**CORD** (verb); a **PRE**-sent / to pre-**SENT**; an **OB**-ject / to ob-**JECT**.
- Words ending in **-tion, -sion, -ic**: stress just before the ending — in-for-**MA**-tion, de-**CI**-sion, e-co-**NO**-mic.
- Words ending in **-ity, -ogy, -graphy**: stress the syllable three from the end — u-ni-**VER**-si-ty, bi-**O**-lo-gy.

steps.title: Words Indian speakers often stress differently
steps.body:
- de-**VE**-lop-ment (not deve-LOP-ment)
- e-**CO**-no-my (not eco-NO-my) — but e-co-**NO**-mic
- com-**PU**-ter
- ho-**TEL**
- **CA**-te-go-ry
- ad-**VER**-tise-ment (British) / ad-ver-**TISE**-ment (American) — both are accepted

Dictionaries show stress with a mark (ˈ) before the stressed syllable — check new words.

steps.title: Practice trick: clap the stress

scenes.text: Karthik's sales pitch in Coimbatore was grammatically perfect but sounded flat; clients drifted off.
His coach marked the key words in his script and showed where his voice should rise and fall.
'Stress the words that carry meaning,' she said, 'and let the little words relax.'
His next pitch sounded lively and confident — and he closed the deal.

steps.title: Sentence stress: content vs function words
steps.body:
English stresses **content words** (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, negatives) and relaxes **function words** (a, the, to, of, and, is, can, for).

'I **WANT** to **GO** to the **MAR**ket on **SUN**day.'

Stress also shows meaning: '**I** didn't take your pen' (someone else did) vs 'I didn't take your **PEN**' (I took something else).

steps.title: Intonation: rising and falling
steps.body:
- **Falling** ↘ for statements and wh- questions: 'I live in Pune. ↘' 'Where do you live? ↘'
- **Rising** ↗ for yes/no questions: 'Are you ready? ↗'
- **Rise-then-fall** in lists: 'I bought apples ↗, bananas ↗ and mangoes ↘.'
- A rising tone on a statement can sound unsure or like a question — useful sometimes, confusing at others.

steps.title: Linking words together
steps.body:
Native-like flow comes from linking:

- **Consonant + vowel**: 'turn‿off' → 'tur-noff', 'an‿apple' → 'a-napple', 'pick‿it‿up' → 'pi-ki-tup'.
- **Weak forms**: 'to' → /tə/, 'and' → /ən/, 'can' → /kən/ when unstressed: 'I can swim' = 'I kən SWIM'.
- But in short answers, use strong forms: 'Yes, I **CAN**.'

steps.title: Shadowing for rhythm
steps.body: Choose a 30-second clip of clear English (news, a TED-style talk, an audiobook). Play one sentence, pause, and repeat it **copying the rhythm, stress and melody**, not just the words. Do 10 minutes daily.

scenes.text: Deepika, a bank clerk in Patna, translated every sentence from Hindi in her head before speaking. She paused for long seconds.
She started a 20-minute daily routine: shadowing, describing her day aloud, and a weekly call with a speaking partner.
She kept a 'phrases I needed' notebook and learned whole chunks, not single words.
In three months, her pauses shrank. 'I stopped translating,' she said. 'I started thinking.'

steps.title: Learn chunks, not just words
steps.body:
Fluent speakers use ready-made **chunks**: 'to be honest', 'as far as I know', 'I was wondering if…', 'it depends on…', 'on the other hand', 'the thing is…'.

Keep a notebook of chunks you hear and needed. Use each in five sentences of your own.

steps.title: A 20-minute daily routine
steps.body:
- **5 min shadowing**: copy a clip sentence by sentence.
- **5 min self-talk**: describe what you're doing ('Now I'm making tea. I'm adding ginger…') or retell a news story.
- **5 min chunk practice**: use three new chunks in your own sentences.
- **5 min recording**: speak on a topic for 1–2 minutes, listen back, note one thing to improve.

Once a week: talk with a partner or join an online conversation group.

steps.title: Handling pauses and mistakes
steps.body:
Use natural fillers instead of silence: 'Well…', 'Let me think…', 'That's a good question…', 'What I mean is…'.

If you make a mistake, **don't stop** — self-correct quickly ('He go— he goes') and carry on. Communication matters more than perfection.

steps.title: Fear of speaking
steps.body: Most learners fear being judged. Start in low-stakes settings (alone, with a friend, an online group), prepare a few lines before important conversations, and breathe slowly before speaking. Every conversation is practice — even awkward ones make you better.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For the next 7 days, do the 20-minute routine. Each day, record one minute on a new topic (my city, my favourite food, my goals). Compare day 1 and day 7.

scenes.text: Harish, an engineering graduate from Salem, answered 'Tell me about yourself' by starting with his school marks and his father's job. Four minutes later, he was still in Class 10.
The interviewer politely moved on. Harish didn't get through.
A career counsellor taught him the Present–Past–Future structure and a 75-second limit.
In his next interview, the panel leaned forward and asked follow-up questions about his project. He got the offer.

steps.title: Present – Past – Future
steps.body:
1. **Present**: who you are now. 'I'm a final-year computer science student at… / I'm a data analyst with two years' experience at…'
2. **Past**: 1–2 relevant achievements. 'During my internship at…, I built a dashboard that cut reporting time by 30%.'
3. **Future**: why this role. 'I'm excited about this role because it combines analytics with customer impact, which is where I want to grow.'

Keep it to **60–90 seconds**. Skip family details, marks from school and hobbies unless they're relevant.

steps.title: Sample answer (fresher)
steps.body: 'I'm a final-year BCom student from Madurai, and I've focused on finance and data. Last summer I interned with a CA firm, where I helped reconcile accounts for 15 small businesses and learned Excel modelling. I also led our college's finance club, organising a stock-market workshop for 200 students. I'm applying for this analyst role because I enjoy turning numbers into decisions, and your team's work with small businesses really interests me.'

steps.title: Indian-English phrases to rethink in interviews
steps.body:
- 'Myself Harish' → 'I'm Harish.'
- 'I am basically from…' → drop 'basically'.
- 'I have done my graduation in…' → 'I graduated in… / I completed my degree in…'
- 'Kindly do the needful' (in emails) → 'Could you please…'
- 'I will revert back' → 'I'll get back to you.' ('Revert' alone is used in Indian business English but may confuse international interviewers.)

steps.title: Delivery matters
steps.body: Sit upright, make eye contact (look at the camera in video interviews), speak a little slower than normal, smile at the start and end. Practise aloud until it sounds natural — not memorised word-for-word.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your Present–Past–Future answer. Time yourself. Cut it until it's under 90 seconds. Record it and watch once.

scenes.text: Swati, applying for a team-lead role in Bengaluru, was asked: 'Tell me about a time you handled a conflict.'
In her first interview she said, 'I'm very good with people,' and stopped.
Before the next interview she prepared five STAR stories: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
This time, her specific story about two developers clashing over a deadline impressed the panel.

steps.title: STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result
steps.body:
- **Situation**: brief context — where, when.
- **Task**: your responsibility or the challenge.
- **Action**: what **you** did (use 'I', not just 'we') — the longest part.
- **Result**: the outcome, ideally with a number, plus what you learned.

Use STAR for 'Tell me about a time when…', 'Give an example of…', 'Describe a situation…'.

steps.title: Sample STAR answer
steps.body:
**S**: 'In my final-year project, our team of four was two weeks behind schedule.'
**T**: 'As team lead, I had to get us back on track without burning people out.'
**A**: 'I broke the remaining work into daily tasks, paired our strongest coder with the member who was stuck, and set a 15-minute daily check-in.'
**R**: 'We submitted on time and scored an A. I learned that small daily visibility prevents big delays.'

steps.title: Tricky questions and how to approach them
steps.body:
- **'What is your weakness?'** → a real, non-critical weakness + what you're doing about it: 'I used to over-prepare slides; now I time-box preparation and get early feedback.'
- **'Why should we hire you?'** → match 2–3 of your strengths to their needs.
- **'Where do you see yourself in five years?'** → growth in skills and responsibility connected to the role.
- **'Why are you leaving your current job?'** → positive, forward-looking; never criticise your employer.
- **'Do you have any questions for us?'** → always yes: 'What does success look like in the first 90 days?'

steps.title: Build a story bank
steps.body: Prepare **5–6 STAR stories** that cover: teamwork, conflict, failure/mistake, leadership, a difficult problem, and handling pressure. One story can answer several questions with a different emphasis.

They both booked 'IELTS' — then wondered whether they needed the same test.
Their teacher explained: Academic for study, General Training usually for work or migration — but always check what your university or immigration body requires.
Each booked the right version and prepared for its specific Reading and Writing tasks.

steps.title: Independent practice material
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Formats and rules can change — always confirm on the official IELTS website before your test.

steps.title: The four parts
steps.body:
- **Listening** (about 30 minutes): 4 parts, 40 questions — conversations and monologues. Paper-based tests add time to transfer answers; computer-delivered tests give a short review period.
- **Reading** (60 minutes): 40 questions. Academic uses texts from books, journals, newspapers; General Training uses everyday and workplace texts.
- **Writing** (60 minutes): **Task 1** (at least 150 words) — Academic: describe a graph, chart, table, map or process; General Training: write a letter. **Task 2** (at least 250 words): an essay. Task 2 carries more weight.
- **Speaking** (11–14 minutes): a face-to-face interview with an examiner in 3 parts — Part 1 familiar topics, Part 2 a long turn (1 minute to prepare, then speak for 1–2 minutes), Part 3 a discussion.

steps.title: Band scores
steps.body:
Each skill is scored on a **band scale from 0 to 9** (half bands like 6.5 are possible). The **overall band** is the average of the four skills, rounded to the nearest half band.

Example: Listening 7, Reading 6.5, Writing 6, Speaking 7 → average 6.625 → overall **6.5**.

Universities and immigration bodies often require a minimum overall band **and** minimum bands in each skill — check your target's exact requirement.

steps.title: How Writing and Speaking are assessed
steps.body:
- **Writing**: Task Achievement (Task 1) / Task Response (Task 2), Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource (vocabulary), Grammatical Range and Accuracy.
- **Speaking**: Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, Pronunciation.

Knowing the criteria tells you exactly what to practise.

steps.title: Speaking strategies
steps.body:
- **Part 1**: answer + reason/example in 2–3 sentences. 'Do you like cooking?' → 'Yes, I do, especially South Indian breakfasts. My mother taught me to make dosas, and now I cook on weekends.'
- **Part 2**: use the 1 minute to note keywords for each bullet point; speak until the examiner stops you — use past experiences, details, feelings.
- **Part 3**: give opinions with reasons and examples; compare past/present, consider different viewpoints: 'On one hand… on the other hand…'.
- It's fine to ask: 'Could you repeat the question, please?' Don't memorise answers — examiners notice.

steps.title: Writing Task 1 (Academic)
steps.body:
1. **Paraphrase** the question in your introduction.
2. Write an **overview**: 2 main trends or key features (essential for a high score).
3. Two body paragraphs with **specific data** grouped logically.
4. No personal opinion.

Useful language: 'rose sharply', 'fell slightly', 'remained stable', 'peaked at', 'accounted for', 'in contrast', 'whereas'.

steps.title: Writing Task 2 (essay)
steps.body:
1. **Plan for ~5 minutes**: identify the question type (opinion, discussion, problem–solution, advantages–disadvantages) and **answer every part**.
2. **Introduction**: paraphrase + your clear position.
3. **Two body paragraphs**: one main idea each, explained and supported with an example.
4. **Conclusion**: restate your position.

Aim for about 260–290 words; leave a few minutes to check articles, verb tenses and plurals.

steps.title: Common mistakes that cap scores
steps.body:
- Memorised, generic introductions and phrases.
- Not answering all parts of the question.
- No overview in Task 1.
- Very long, unclear sentences with errors — accuracy beats complexity.
- Under the word count.
- In Speaking: very short answers, or reciting prepared speeches.

steps.title: How the script works
steps.body:
Tamil is written in the **Tamil script**, **left to right**, with rounded letters and **no top line**. It has **12 vowels and 18 consonants** (plus a special letter ஃ), which combine into many syllable letters.

Tamil script doesn't have separate letters for many voiced/voiceless pairs: the same letter **க** can sound like *k* (at the start of a word) or *g/h* (between vowels). You learn the pattern by listening.

steps.title: The famous ழ (zh) sound
steps.body:
The letter **ழ** is a special sound: curl your tongue back (like an English 'r') and let it glide, close to an 'l'. It appears in **தமிழ் Tamizh** and **பழம் pazham** (fruit). Transliteration often writes it as *zh* or *ḻ*.

Tamil also distinguishes **ல l / ள ḷ / ழ zh** and **ர r / ற ṟ** — listen carefully to native speakers.

steps.title: About Tamil
steps.body:
- About **6.9 crore** people in India reported Tamil as their mother tongue in Census 2011; it is also an official language in **Sri Lanka** and **Singapore**.
- Official language of **Tamil Nadu** and **Puducherry**.
- In **2004**, Tamil became the **first language declared a classical language** by the Government of India; its literature goes back over two thousand years (Sangam literature).
- Tamil has notable **diglossia**: formal written Tamil and everyday spoken Tamil differ. This course uses polite spoken forms.

steps.title: Core greetings
steps.body:
- **வணக்கம்** — *vanakkam* — hello / greetings (respectful, any time of day)
- **எப்படி இருக்கீங்க?** — *eppadi irukeenga?* — how are you? (polite spoken)
- **நல்லா இருக்கேன்** — *nalla irukken* — I'm fine
- **நன்றி** — *nandri* — thank you
- **போயிட்டு வரேன்** — *poyittu varen* — bye (literally 'I'll go and come back')

steps.title: Introducing yourself
steps.body:

steps.title: Respect: நீங்க(ள்) and நீ
steps.body:
- **நீங்கள் neengal** (spoken **neenga**) — respectful (and plural). **Use by default.**
- **நீ nee** — informal: close friends, children.

Adding **-nga** to verbs makes requests polite: *vaanga* (please come), *ukkaarunga* (please sit), *sollunga* (please say).

steps.title: Culture tip
steps.body: **Pongal** (the harvest festival in January) and **Tamil New Year** (Puthandu, in April) are big celebrations. Elders are often addressed as *Paati* (grandmother) and *Thatha* (grandfather); *Anna* (elder brother) and *Akka* (elder sister) are friendly ways to address people a little older than you.

steps.title: Grammar note

steps.title: How the script works
steps.body: Telugu has its **own rounded script**, written **left to right**, closely related to the **Kannada** script. Many letters have a small tick or curl on top. Like other Indian scripts, consonants carry a built-in vowel and **vowel signs** change it.

steps.title: A vowel-ending language
steps.body: Most native Telugu words **end in a vowel**: *illu* (house), *neellu* (water), *pani* (work), *padi* (ten). This gives Telugu its flowing, musical sound. Telugu also has **retroflex** sounds (ట ṭa, డ ḍa, ణ ṇa) — tongue curled back — and dental sounds (త ta, ద da) with the tongue at the teeth.

steps.title: About Telugu
steps.body:
- About **8.1 crore** people in India reported Telugu as their mother tongue in Census 2011 — one of the most spoken languages in India.
- Official language of **Andhra Pradesh** and **Telangana**.
- Declared a **classical language** by the Government of India in **2008**.

steps.title: How Devanagari works
steps.body:
Hindi is written in **Devanagari**, from **left to right**. Most letters hang from a **top line** (shirorekha).

Each consonant carries a built-in **'a'** sound: क = ka, म = ma, न = na. To change the vowel, you add a **vowel sign (matra)**:

- क ka · का kaa · कि ki · की kee · कु ku · कू koo · के ke · कै kai · को ko · कौ kau

So you learn ~11 vowel signs once, and they work with every consonant.

steps.title: Sounds that matter
steps.body:
- **Aspirated vs unaspirated**: क ka (no puff) / ख kha (with a puff of air); प pa / फ pha. Hold a paper in front of your mouth — it moves for kha, pha.
- **Dental vs retroflex**: त ta (tongue touches the teeth) / ट ṭa (tongue curled back). Similarly द da / ड ḍa.
- **Nasal vowels**: the dot or moon sign (ं ँ) adds a nasal sound, as in हाँ haan (yes).

In transliteration, long vowels are often written double: aa, ee, oo.

steps.title: About Hindi
steps.body:
- In Census 2011, about **52.8 crore** people in India reported Hindi (including many related regional speech forms) as their mother tongue — the largest in India.
- Hindi in Devanagari is the **official language of the Union**, with English also used for official purposes.
- Everyday spoken Hindi and Urdu share most grammar and basic vocabulary; Urdu is written in a Perso-Arabic script.

steps.title: Respect: आप, तुम, तू
steps.body:
Hindi has three words for 'you':

- **आप aap** — respectful: elders, strangers, at work. **Use this by default.**
- **तुम tum** — familiar: friends, younger people.
- **तू too** — very intimate (close family, small children); can sound rude to others.

Adding **जी ji** after a name or 'haan' (haan ji) adds warmth and respect.

steps.title: Gender in Hindi
steps.body:
Nouns are masculine or feminine, and many verbs and adjectives change to match the **speaker or subject**:

- A man says: मैं चाय पीता हूँ — *main chaay peeta hoon* — I drink tea.
- A woman says: मैं चाय पीती हूँ — *main chaay peeti hoon*.

Don't worry about mistakes — people will understand and appreciate the effort.

steps.title: How the script works
steps.body:
Bengali is written in the **Bengali (Bangla) script**, **left to right**, with letters hanging from a **top line** — similar in design to Devanagari but with different letter shapes.

Like Devanagari, each consonant carries a built-in vowel, and **vowel signs** change it. In Bengali, that built-in vowel usually sounds like a short **'o'** (as in 'hot'), not 'a' — which is why names like *Kolkata* and words like *kemon* sound the way they do.

steps.title: Sound features
steps.body:
- **Aspirated pairs**: ক ko / খ kho, প po / ফ pho.
- The letter স and its relatives are often pronounced **'sh'**: সাত sounds like *shaat* (seven).
- Bengali has its own digits: ১ ২ ৩ ৪ ৫ ৬ ৭ ৮ ৯ ০, though everyday life also uses 1, 2, 3.

steps.title: About Bengali
steps.body:
- About **9.7 crore** people in India reported Bengali as their mother tongue in Census 2011; it is the national language of **Bangladesh**.
- Official language of **West Bengal** and **Tripura** (and used in parts of Assam).
- Rabindranath Tagore wrote in Bengali; India's national anthem was originally written by him in Bengali.
- The Government of India declared Bengali a **classical language** in 2024.
- **Grammar bonus**: Bengali verbs do **not** change for the gender of the speaker — easier than Hindi!

steps.title: Same script, Marathi style
steps.body:
Marathi is written in **Devanagari**, left to right, with the top line — the same basic letters and vowel signs as Hindi. A few things stand out:

- The letter **ळ (ḷa)** — an 'l' made with the tongue curled back — is very common: *शाळा shaala* (school), *वेळ vel* (time).
- **ण (ṇa)**, a retroflex 'n', appears often: *पाणी paani* (water).

steps.title: Three genders
steps.body:
Marathi nouns can be **masculine, feminine or neuter**, and verbs and adjectives agree. For example, saying 'I am fine':

- Man: **मी बरा आहे** — *mee bara aahe*
- Woman: **मी बरी आहे** — *mee bari aahe*

steps.title: About Marathi
steps.body:
- About **8.3 crore** people in India reported Marathi as their mother tongue in Census 2011.
- Official language of **Maharashtra**; also spoken in Goa and neighbouring states.
- Declared a **classical language** by the Government of India in 2024.
- Marathi literature includes the saint-poets (Sant Dnyaneshwar, Sant Tukaram) whose abhangs are still sung.

steps.title: How the script works
steps.body:
Gujarati has its **own script**, closely related to Devanagari, written **left to right** — but **without the top line** (shirorekha). Many letters look like Devanagari letters with the line removed and slightly reshaped.

It works the same way: each consonant has a built-in 'a' and **vowel signs** change it: ક ka, કા kaa, કિ ki, કી kee, કુ ku, કે ke, કો ko.

steps.title: Grammar features
steps.body: Gujarati has **three genders** (masculine, feminine, neuter) and **SOV** word order. Adjectives and some verb forms agree with gender — but beginners are understood even with small mistakes.

- Mahatma Gandhi wrote his autobiography originally in Gujarati.

steps.title: Gurmukhi
steps.body:
In India, Punjabi is written in **Gurmukhi** script, **left to right**, with a **top line**. Like Devanagari, consonants carry a built-in vowel and **vowel signs** modify it.

In Pakistan, Punjabi is mostly written in **Shahmukhi**, a Perso-Arabic script. Same language, two scripts.

steps.title: Tones and double consonants
steps.body:
- Punjabi is one of the few **tonal** Indo-Aryan languages: the **pitch** of a syllable (level, rising or falling) can distinguish words. Learn tones by listening and imitating — transliteration can't show them well.
- Punjabi has many **doubled (geminated) consonants**, marked by the sign ੱ (addak): ਇੱਕ *ikk* (one), ਸੱਤ *satt* (seven). Hold the consonant a little longer.

steps.title: About Punjabi
steps.body:
- About **3.3 crore** people in India reported Punjabi as their mother tongue in Census 2011; it is also widely spoken in Pakistan and by large communities in Canada, the UK and elsewhere.
- Official language of **Punjab**; also an additional official language in some neighbouring areas.
- The Sikh scripture, **Guru Granth Sahib**, is written in Gurmukhi script.

steps.title: Five pure vowels
steps.body:
Spanish uses the Latin alphabet and has **five short, pure vowels**, always pronounced the same way:

- **a** as in 'father' · **e** as in 'get' · **i** as in 'machine' · **o** as in 'for' (short) · **u** as in 'rule'

Unlike English, the vowels don't change much from word to word — that's why Spanish spelling is so regular.

steps.title: Special letters and sounds
steps.body:
- **ñ** = 'ny' as in 'canyon': *España*, *mañana* (tomorrow).
- **j** (and **g** before e/i) = a throaty 'h': *jardín*, *gente*.
- **h** is **silent**: *hola* = 'o-la'.
- **ll** and **y** usually sound like 'y': *llamo* ('yamo').
- **rr** is a rolled 'r' — like the Indian rolled r in many languages, which helps Indian learners!
- **¿ ¡**: questions and exclamations start with upside-down marks: *¿Cómo estás?* *¡Hola!*
- An accent mark (á, é, í, ó, ú) shows which syllable is stressed: *café*, *teléfono*.

steps.title: Silent final letters
steps.body: Many final consonants are **not pronounced**: *Paris* ('pa-ree'), *petit* ('puh-tee'), *beaucoup* ('bo-koo'), *vous* ('voo'). A final **-e** is usually silent too. Common exceptions: final **c, r, f, l** are often pronounced (think of the word *CaReFuL*): *avec, bonjour, neuf, il*.

steps.title: Nasal vowels and the French r
steps.body:
- **Nasal vowels**: *on, an/en, in/ain, un* — air goes through the nose and the n isn't fully pronounced: *bon* ('bõ'), *pain* (bread), *enfant* (child). Indian learners often find these familiar from nasal sounds in Hindi (हाँ).
- **r** is made at the back of the throat, a soft gargle: *merci, Paris*.
- **u** (as in *tu*): say 'ee' with rounded lips.

steps.title: Accents and linking
steps.body:
- **é** = 'ay' (*café*), **è/ê** = 'e' as in 'bed' (*mère*, *fête*), **ç** = 's' (*français*).
- **Liaison**: a normally silent final consonant is pronounced before a vowel: *vous avez* ('voo-za-vay').

scenes.text: Siddharth, a mechanical engineering graduate in Coimbatore, plans to apply for a master's in Germany.
He starts learning German and is confused: 'Why does Wasser sound like Vasser?'
His online tutor, Frau Becker, explains a few spelling rules — and German suddenly looks logical.
Within a month he reads German signs on Google Street View for fun.

steps.title: Letters that surprise English speakers
steps.body:
- **w** = English 'v': *Wasser* ('vasser', water), *wie* ('vee', how).
- **v** often = 'f': *Vater* ('fahter', father), *vier* ('feer', four).
- **j** = 'y': *ja* ('yah', yes).
- **z** = 'ts': *zehn* ('tsayn', ten).
- **ei** = 'eye': *drei* (three), *nein* (no). **ie** = 'ee': *vier*, *Bier*.
- **ch** after a, o, u is a throaty sound (*Bach*); after e, i it's softer (*ich*).

steps.title: Umlauts and ß
steps.body:
- **ä** ≈ 'e' in 'bed' · **ö** = say 'ay' with rounded lips · **ü** = say 'ee' with rounded lips (like French u).
- **ß** (Eszett) = 'ss': *Straße* (street), *heißen* (to be called).

steps.title: Capital nouns and three genders
steps.body:
- **All nouns are capitalised**: *das Haus* (the house), *der Tisch* (the table).
- German has **three genders**: **der** (masculine), **die** (feminine), **das** (neuter). *Die* is also used for all plurals. Learn every noun with its article.

steps.title: About German
steps.body: German is an official language of **Germany, Austria, Switzerland** (one of four national languages), **Liechtenstein, Luxembourg** and **Belgium** (one of three). Germany is a popular destination for Indian students, especially in engineering and science.

steps.title: du or Sie?
steps.body:
- **du** — informal: friends, family, children, fellow students.
- **Sie** (always with a capital S) — formal: strangers, officials, professors, at work until invited to use du.

Use **Sie** with adults you don't know; Germans will often say if they prefer du.

steps.title: Culture tip
steps.body: Punctuality is valued in Germany — arrive on time for appointments. A firm handshake and eye contact are common in formal greetings; titles like *Herr* (Mr.) and *Frau* (Ms./Mrs.) are used with surnames: *Guten Tag, Frau Becker*.

scenes.text: Kabir, 13, in Delhi loves anime and wants to understand without subtitles.
He opens a Japanese book and sees three different kinds of characters on one page.
His online teacher, Tanaka-sensei, explains: 'Hiragana, katakana and kanji — each has a job.'
Kabir writes his name in katakana: カビール. He's hooked.

steps.title: Hiragana, katakana, kanji
steps.body:
- **Hiragana** (ひらがな): 46 basic characters, each a syllable (*a, ka, sa…*). Used for grammar endings, particles and native words.
- **Katakana** (カタカナ): the same sounds in a sharper style — used for **foreign words and names**: インド *Indo* (India), コーヒー *kōhī* (coffee).
- **Kanji** (漢字): characters that came from Chinese, each carrying meaning: 山 (mountain), 水 (water), 日本 (Japan).

A sentence usually mixes all three. Beginners start with hiragana.

steps.title: Sounds
steps.body: Japanese has **five vowels** — a, i, u, e, o — pronounced short and pure (like Hindi अ इ उ ए ओ). Syllables are mostly **consonant + vowel**: *ka-ra-o-ke*, *su-shi*. A line over a vowel in romaji (ō, ū) means it's **long** — hold it twice as long: *Tōkyō*.

steps.title: About Japanese
steps.body: Japanese is spoken mainly in **Japan**. Its grammar is **subject–object–verb**, like Hindi: *watashi wa ringo o tabemasu* — I apple eat (= I eat an apple). Indian learners often find the word order surprisingly natural.

steps.title: Try this

steps.title: Greetings
steps.body:
- **おはようございます** — *ohayō gozaimasu* — good morning (polite)
- **こんにちは** — *konnichiwa* — hello / good afternoon
- **こんばんは** — *konbanwa* — good evening
- **ありがとうございます** — *arigatō gozaimasu* — thank you (polite)
- **すみません** — *sumimasen* — excuse me / sorry
- **さようなら** — *sayōnara* — goodbye (rather formal; friends say **じゃあね** *jā ne* or **またね** *mata ne* — see you)

steps.title: Introducing yourself
steps.body:
- **はじめまして** — *hajimemashite* — nice to meet you (said at a first meeting)
- **わたしは ___ です** — *watashi wa ___ desu* — I am ___
- **インドから きました** — *Indo kara kimashita* — I came from India
- **よろしく おねがいします** — *yoroshiku onegaishimasu* — 'please treat me kindly' — said at the end of an introduction

Note: the particle は is pronounced **wa** when it marks the topic.

steps.title: Politeness and -san
steps.body:
- Add **-san** after other people's names (never your own): *Tanaka-san*.
- **desu / -masu** endings are the polite style — use them with people you don't know well.
- A light **bow** is a normal greeting; a deeper bow shows more respect or apology.

steps.title: Culture tip
steps.body: Take off your shoes when entering homes (and some temples and restaurants). Before eating, people say **いただきます** *itadakimasu*, and after eating **ごちそうさまでした** *gochisōsama deshita* — expressing thanks for the food.

scenes.text: Faisal, an electrician from Kozhikode, gets a job in Dubai.
Signs are in Arabic and English. He wants to read the Arabic too.
His supervisor, Omar, explains: 'We write right to left, and most letters join their neighbours.'

steps.title: Right to left, joined letters
steps.body:
Arabic is written **from right to left**. It has **28 letters**, and most letters **join** to the next one, changing shape slightly depending on whether they're at the start, middle or end of a word (or standing alone).

Short vowels are usually **not written** in everyday text — readers know them from context. Children's books and religious texts often add small vowel marks.

steps.title: Sounds new to many learners
steps.body:
- **ع** (ʿayn) — a deep sound from the throat.
- **ح** (ḥā') — a breathy 'h' from the throat.
- **خ** (khā') — like 'kh' in *khana* (Urdu/Hindi) — familiar to many Indian learners!
- **ق** (qāf) — a 'k' made further back, like *q* in Urdu *qalam*.

Many Arabic words entered Hindi and Urdu through Persian: *kitāb* (book), *dunyā* (world), *waqt* (time).

steps.title: About Arabic
steps.body: Arabic is an official language in more than 20 countries across West Asia and North Africa and one of the six official languages of the United Nations. **Modern Standard Arabic** is used in news, books and formal settings; people speak regional **dialects** at home. Many Indians live and work in Gulf countries where Arabic is the official language.

scenes.text: On his first day, Faisal meets the site manager, Mr. Khalid.
'As-salāmu ʿalaykum!' says Faisal. 'Wa ʿalaykumu s-salām!' replies Mr. Khalid.
'Kayfa ḥāluk?' 'Bi-khayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh. Ismī Faisal.'
'Tasharrafnā, Faisal!' The manager is pleased he made the effort.

steps.title: Core greetings
steps.body:
- **السلام عليكم** — *as-salāmu ʿalaykum* — peace be upon you (a very common greeting) → reply **وعليكم السلام** — *wa ʿalaykumu s-salām* — and upon you peace
- **مرحبا** — *marḥaban* — hello
- **صباح الخير** — *ṣabāḥ al-khayr* — good morning → reply **صباح النور** — *ṣabāḥ an-nūr*
- **مساء الخير** — *masāʾ al-khayr* — good evening → reply **مساء النور** — *masāʾ an-nūr*
- **مع السلامة** — *maʿa s-salāma* — goodbye

steps.title: How are you? and introductions
steps.body:
- **كيف حالك؟** — *kayfa ḥāluk?* (to a man) / *kayfa ḥāluki?* (to a woman) — how are you?
- **بخير، الحمد لله** — *bi-khayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh* — fine, praise be to God (a very common reply)
- **اسمي ___** — *ismī ___* — my name is ___
- **ما اسمك؟** — *mā ismuk?* (to a man) / *mā ismuki?* (to a woman) — what's your name?
- **أنا من الهند** — *anā min al-hind* — I'm from India
- **تشرفنا** — *tasharrafnā* — pleased to meet you

steps.title: Masculine and feminine 'you'
steps.body: Arabic changes words depending on whether you speak **to a man or a woman**: *ḥāluk* / *ḥāluki*, *ismuk* / *ismuki*. *Shukran* (thank you) stays the same for everyone.

steps.title: Culture tip
steps.body: Hospitality is important: you may be offered coffee or tea — accepting is polite. Use the right hand for eating, giving and receiving. In conservative settings, wait for a person of the opposite gender to offer a handshake first.

Many Arab countries use **Eastern Arabic digits**: ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥ ٦ ٧ ٨ ٩ ١٠. The digits we call 'Arabic numerals' (1, 2, 3) are also widely used, especially in North Africa and on many Gulf price tags.

steps.title: Numbers go left to right!
steps.body: Even though Arabic text runs right to left, **numbers are written left to right**: ٢٥ = 25. So in a sentence your eyes jump direction for numbers.

steps.title: Market tip
steps.body: Bargaining is common in traditional souks (markets) but not in malls and supermarkets. Polite, friendly bargaining is part of the experience.

lessons.title: Survival phrases and a real conversation

scenes.text: On his day off, Faisal wants to visit a friend and needs the metro.
'Min faḍlak, ayna l-mitrū?' he asks a shopkeeper.
The answer is fast, in a Gulf dialect. 'Lā afham. Bi-buṭʾ, min faḍlak.'
The shopkeeper smiles, repeats slowly and points: 'Yamīn.' Right. 'Shukran!'

steps.title: Phrases that get you through
steps.body:
- **عفوا / المعذرة** — *ʿafwan / al-maʿdhira* — excuse me
- **آسف / آسفة** — *āsif / āsifa* — sorry (said by a man / a woman)
- **لا أفهم** — *lā afham* — I don't understand
- **ببطء من فضلك** — *bi-buṭʾ min faḍlak* — slowly, please
- **أين ___؟** — *ayna ___?* — where is ___? (*al-ḥammām* — the toilet)
- **ماء** — *māʾ* — water
- **نعم / لا** — *naʿam / lā* — yes / no
- **ساعدني من فضلك** — *sāʿidnī min faḍlak* — help me, please · **هل تتكلم الإنجليزية؟** — *hal tatakallam al-injlīziyya?* — do you speak English? (to a man)

steps.title: Directions
steps.body:
- **يمين** — *yamīn* — right · **يسار** — *yasār* — left
- **قريب** — *qarīb* — near · **بعيد** — *baʿīd* — far
- For 'straight ahead' you'll hear different expressions by region; a widely understood colloquial one is **على طول** *ʿalā ṭūl*.

steps.title: Dialects are normal
steps.body: People in the Gulf, Egypt, the Levant and North Africa speak different dialects. If someone answers in dialect, it's fine to say *lā afham* and ask them to speak slowly — most people will switch to simpler words or English.

Japanese has three scripts; hiragana is the first to learn: each symbol is one sound (a mora).

steps.title: The five vowels
steps.body: あ **a**, い **i**, う **u**, え **e**, お **o**. Japanese vowels are short and pure.

steps.title: Next rows
steps.body: K: か ka, き ki, く ku, け ke, こ ko. S: さ sa, し shi, す su, せ se, そ so. T: た ta, ち chi, つ tsu, て te, と to. N: な na, に ni, ぬ nu, ね ne, の no.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing さ/ち and similar-looking shapes; practise stroke order.
- Reading う as English "oo" with lip rounding; it is a relaxed u.

steps.title: H and M rows
steps.body: H: は ha, ひ hi, ふ fu, へ he, ほ ho. M: ま ma, み mi, む mu, め me, も mo.

steps.title: Y, R, W and N
steps.body: Y: や ya, ゆ yu, よ yo. R: ら ra, り ri, る ru, れ re, ろ ro. W: わ wa, を wo (the object particle, pronounced o). ん n.

steps.title: Voicing marks
steps.body: Add two small strokes (dakuten ゛) to voice: か → が ga, さ → ざ za, た → だ da, は → ば ba; a small circle (handakuten ゜) gives ぱ pa. Small ゃ ゅ ょ combine: き + ゃ = きゃ kya. A small っ doubles the next consonant: ざっし zasshi.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading は as "ha" when it is the topic particle (pronounced wa).
- Forgetting that を is only for the object particle.

steps.title: Sentence frame
steps.body: X は Y です = X is Y. わたし は ミーラ です (watashi wa Mīra desu) = I am Meera. これ は みず です (kore wa mizu desu) = This is water. Question: ～ですか (…desu ka?).

steps.title: Numbers and price
steps.body: いち 1, に 2, さん 3, よん 4, ご 5, ろく 6, なな 7, はち 8, きゅう 9, じゅう 10. いくら ですか (ikura desu ka?) = How much is it? えん (en) = yen: ひゃくえん = 100 yen.

steps.title: Particles
steps.body: を marks the object: みず を ください (mizu o kudasai) = Water, please. に marks destination/time: えき に いきます (eki ni ikimasu) = I go to the station. で marks place of action: うち で たべます (uchi de tabemasu) = I eat at home.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using よん/なな inconsistently; both 4 and 7 have two readings, learn the common ones.
- Adding "desu" after a question word incorrectly; remember the ka.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Dictionary form → polite: たべる → たべます (tabemasu, eat), いく → いきます (ikimasu, go), のむ → のみます (nomimasu, drink), みる → みます (mimasu, see). Negative: ～ません (tabemasen). Past: ～ました (tabemashita); past negative ～ませんでした.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body: わたし は パン を たべます。 I eat bread. あした きょうと に いきます。 I will go to Kyoto tomorrow. Japanese verbs do not change for person.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Putting the verb in the middle; Japanese is subject–object–verb.

lessons.title: Hangul: consonants, vowels and syllable blocks

story.title: The alphabet designed to be learned

scenes.text: Hangul was created in the 15th century; it is built logically from sound shapes.
Each syllable block has an initial consonant, a vowel and sometimes a final consonant.

steps.title: Basic letters
steps.body: Consonants: ㄱ g/k, ㄴ n, ㄷ d/t, ㄹ r/l, ㅁ m, ㅂ b/p, ㅅ s, ㅇ (silent at the start, "ng" at the end), ㅈ j. Vowels: ㅏ a, ㅓ eo, ㅗ o, ㅜ u, ㅡ eu, ㅣ i.

steps.title: Building blocks
steps.body: ㄴ + ㅏ = 나 na. ㅁ + ㅜ + ㄹ = 물 mul (water). ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한 han. Vertical vowels (ㅏ ㅓ ㅣ) go to the right of the consonant; horizontal vowels (ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ) go below. ㅇ is silent at the beginning: 아 = a.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading ㅇ as a sound at the start of a syllable.
- Mixing ㅓ (eo, like "uh") with ㅗ (o).

steps.title: Introduce

steps.title: Vowels (स्वर)
steps.body: अ a, आ ā, इ i, ई ī, उ u, ऊ ū, ऋ ṛ, ए e, ऐ ai, ओ o, औ au. Long vowels (ā ī ū) take about twice the time of short ones. Anusvāra ं (ṃ) and visarga ः (ḥ) are added signs: नमः namaḥ.

scenes.text: Kabir's deaf classmate, Aarav, signs fluently to his family and an interpreter.

steps.title: What ISL is
steps.body: Indian Sign Language is the natural visual–gestural language used by Deaf communities across India. It is **not** a word-for-word signing of Hindi or English and has its own grammar, vocabulary and regional variation. Many Deaf people write "Deaf" with a capital D to show membership of a linguistic and cultural community.

steps.title: Who supports it
steps.body: The **Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre (ISLRTC)** in New Delhi, an autonomous body under the government, works on standardising, researching and teaching ISL, producing an online ISL dictionary and training interpreters and teachers. For authentic signs always learn from ISLRTC materials and Deaf teachers rather than from memory of videos or apps of uncertain origin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying "sign language is universal"; each country has its own.
- Using made-up gestures for school signs; learn the official or local Deaf-community sign.
- Assuming that every Deaf person lip-reads well; lip-reading is only partly reliable.

steps.title: Five parameters
steps.body: 1) **Handshape**, 2) **location** (where on or near the body or in space), 3) **movement** (direction, repetition, speed), 4) **palm orientation** (palm facing up, down, towards the signer, away), 5) **non-manual features** (eyebrows, mouth shape, head tilt, eye gaze). Changing one parameter can change the meaning.

steps.title: Handshape vocabulary in words
steps.body: Describe shapes plainly: **flat hand** (fingers together and straight), **fist** (all fingers curled in), **index point** (one finger extended, others curled), **V-shape** (index and middle fingers spread, others curled), **C-shape** (fingers and thumb curved like the letter C), **O-shape** (fingertips meeting the thumb), **open spread hand** (all fingers apart). These are descriptive categories, not a list of signs.

steps.title: Worked description
steps.body: "Flat hand, palm facing the signer, touching the chest once, small downward movement, eyebrows neutral." Describing like this helps you ask a Deaf teacher precise questions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Describing only the hands and ignoring the face.
- Assuming "same handshape = same meaning".

steps.title: Basics
steps.body: Face the person, make eye contact, keep your mouth visible and speak naturally (do not shout or exaggerate). Use clear gestures, a pen and paper or a phone notes app, and write short, plain sentences. Ask how the person prefers to communicate.

steps.title: Interpreters
steps.body: A qualified ISL interpreter conveys messages between languages. Speak to the Deaf person, not to the interpreter; the interpreter says "I" for the person. Allow pauses and avoid private side conversations. Interpreters are not family members: for medical, legal and educational settings use qualified interpreters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Asking a child to interpret.
- Looking at the interpreter instead of the Deaf person.
- Saying "never mind" when the message does not land; try another way.

steps.title: Fingerspelling
steps.body: Fingerspelling spells words letter by letter using a manual alphabet. In Indian sign language communities many letters are formed with two hands, unlike some other countries' one-handed alphabets; learn the exact forms from ISLRTC material. It is used for names, places and terms without a sign; it is not a replacement for signing.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body: Video calls, captioning apps and messaging help, but captions can be inaccurate. Check understanding; ask for clarification.

steps.title: Rights
steps.body: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 recognises the rights of persons with hearing disabilities and promotes accessibility, including sign language interpretation in various services. For specific help, contact local disability offices and Deaf associations; this is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Spelling everything instead of signing.
- Assuming captions are perfect.

lessons.title: The Braille cell and the first ten letters

scenes.text: Kabir touches a lift button panel with raised dots and wonders how blind people read.
Louis Braille (1809–1852) devised the code as a teenager in France.

steps.title: The cell
steps.body: A cell has six dots in two columns of three. Left column top to bottom: dots 1, 2, 3. Right column: dots 4, 5, 6. Each dot can be raised or not: 2⁶ = 64 patterns, of which 63 are non-blank symbols.

steps.title: Letters a–j
steps.body: a = dot 1. b = dots 1,2. c = dots 1,4. d = dots 1,4,5. e = dots 1,5. f = dots 1,2,4. g = dots 1,2,4,5. h = dots 1,2,5. i = dots 2,4. j = dots 2,4,5.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Letters k–t repeat a–j with **dot 3 added** (k = a + 3 → dots 1,3). u–z (except w) add dots 3 and 6. Numbers: the number sign (dots 3,4,5,6) followed by a–j gives 1–9 and 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Braille is a language; it is a writing system (code) that can write any language.
- Mixing up dot numbers; always count down the left column first.

steps.title: Writing
steps.body: On a slate and stylus, dots are punched from the back so the writer works right to left with mirrored dots; the reader reads left to right on the raised side. A Perkins brailler types all six dots with six keys. Refreshable Braille displays and screen readers also help.

steps.title: Indian context
steps.body: **Bharati Braille** is the unified Braille code for Indian languages, mapping Indic sounds onto the same cell patterns, which lets readers move between Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and other languages. The National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Visual Disabilities (NIEPVD) and other organisations support Braille education.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing left to right on a slate; with a slate you write right to left.
- Forgetting the number sign before a–j.
